'''bel'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''bell''; < ME. ''bele'', ''bel-'', < OF. (and mod. F.) ''bel'', ''beau'', fem. ''belle'', < L. ''bellus'', fair, fine, beautiful: see ''beau'', ''beauty'', ''bel''<sup>5</sup>, etc.] '''1.''' Fair; fine; beautiful.—'''2.''' [Lit. fair, good, as in ''beausire'', fair sir, ''beaupere'', good father, used in F. and ME. to indicate indirect or adopted secondary relationship; so in mod. F. ''beau-'' as a formative in relation-names, ‘step-’, ‘-in-law’; ME. ''bel-'', ‘grand-’, as in ''beldame'', grandmother, ''belsire'', grandfather, also with purely E. names, ''belmoder'', ''belfader'', and later ''belchild''. Cf. Sc. and North. E. ''goodmother'', ''goodfather'', etc., mother-in-law, father-in-law, etc.] Grand-: a formative in relation-names, as ''belsire'', grandfather, ''beldam'', grandmother, etc. See etymology.

'''Bel'''<sup>2</sup> (bel), ''n.'' Same as ''Belus.''

'''bel'''<sup>3</sup> (bel), ''n.'' [Also written, less prop., ''bhel'', ''bael'', repr. Hind. ''bel.''] The East Indian name of the Bengal quince-tree, ''Ægle Marmelos.'' See ''Ægle'', 1.

'''bela''' (bē′lä), ''n.'' [Hind.] The Hindustani name of a species of jasmin, ''Jasminum Sambac'', which is often cultivated for its very fragrant flowers.

'''belabor, belabour''' (bē-lā′bo̤r), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''labor.''] '''1†.''' To work hard upon; ply diligently.
{{smaller block|If the earth is ''belaboured'' with culture, it yieldeth corn.
{{right|''Barrow'', Works, III. xviii.}}}}
'''2.''' To beat soundly; thump.
{{smaller block|They so cudgelled and ''belabored'' him bodily that he might perhaps have lost his life in the encounter had he not been protected by the more respectable portion of the assembly.
{{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, I. 545.}}}}

'''bel-accoil†, bel-accoyle†''' (bel-a-koil′), ''n.'' [< OF. ''bel acoil'', fair welcome: see ''bel''<sup>1</sup> and ''accoil.''] Kindly greeting or reception. ''Spenser.''

'''belace<sup>1</sup>''' (bẹ̄-lās′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''lace.''] '''1.''' To fasten as with a lace or cord.—'''2.''' To adorn with lace.
{{smaller block|<poem>When thou in thy bravest
And most ''belaced'' servitude dost strut,
Some newer fashion doth usurp.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, xvi. 10.}}}}
'''3†.''' To beat; whip. ''Wright.''

'''belace<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' An error (by misprint or confusion with ''belace''<sup>1</sup>) in Bailey and subsequent dictionaries for ''belage'' or ''belay''. See ''belage''.

'''belacedness''' (bẹ̄-lā′sed-nes), ''n.'' In ''math.'', the number of times one branch of a lacing must be passed through another to undo it.

'''beladle''' (bẹ̄-lā′dl), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ladle.''] To pour out with a ladle; ladle out.
{{smaller block|The honest masters of the roast ''beladling'' the dripping.
{{right|''Thackeray.''}}}}

'''belady''' (bẹ̄-lā′di), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''beladied'', ppr. ''beladying''. [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''lady''; cf. ''belord'', ''begrace'', ''beknight''.] To address by the title Lady, or the phrase “my lady.”

'''belage†''', ''v.'' [Either a misprint for ''belaye'', ''belay'', or less prob. a phonetic variant of that word (ME. ''beleggen'', etc.): see ''belay''.] ''Naut.'', to belay. ''Phillips'' (1678); ''Kersey''.

'''belam''' (bẹ̄-lam′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''lam.''] To beat; bang. ''Sherwood.'' [North. Eng.]

'''belcher<sup>2</sup>''' (bel′chėr), ''n.'' [So called from an English pugilist named Jim ''Belcher''.] A neckerchief with darkish-blue ground and large white spots with a dark-blue spot in the center of each. [Slang.]

'''belchild†''' (bel′child), ''n.''; pl. ''belchildren'' (-chil″-dre̤n). [< ''bel-'', grand-, as in ''beldam'', ''belsire'', etc. (see ''bel''<sup>1</sup>), + ''child''.] A grandchild.
{{smaller block|To Thomas Doubledaye and Katherine his wife, my daughter, a cowe. To their children, my ''belchildren'', etc.
{{right|''Will of'' 1564, quoted in N. and Q., 7th ser., III. 77.}}}}

'''beldam, beldame''' (bel′dam, -dām), ''n.'' [< ME. ''beldam'', ''beldame'', only in sense of grandmother (correlative to ''belsire'', grandfather), < ME. ''bel-'', grand-, as in ''belsire'', etc. (see ''bel''<sup>1</sup>), + ''dame'', mother. The word was thus in E. use lit. ‘good mother,’ used distinctively for grandmother, not as in F. ''belle dame'', lit. fair lady: see ''bel''<sup>1</sup>, ''belle'', and ''dame''.] '''1†.''' Grandmother: corresponding to ''belsire'', grandfather: sometimes applied to a great-grandmother.
{{smaller block|To show the ''beldame'' daughters of her daughter.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 953.}}}}
'''2.''' An old woman in general, especially an ugly old woman; a hag.
{{smaller block|Around the ''beldam'' all erect they hang. {{right|''Akenside.''}}
<poem>Our witches are no longer old
And wrinkled ''beldames'', Satan-sold.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', New-England Legend.}}}}
'''3†.''' [A forced use of the F. ''belle dame''.] Fair dame or lady. ''Spenser.''

'''belead†''', ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''beleden'', < AS. ''belǣdan'', < ''be-'' + ''lǣdan'', lead: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''lead''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To lead
readings.c3s3:
away.—'''2.''' To lead; conduct.

'''beleaguer''' (bē-lē′gėr), ''v. t.'' [< D. ''belegeren'', besiege (= G. ''belagern'' = Sw. ''belägra'' = Dan. ''belægre'', also ''belejre'', perhaps < D. ''belegeren''), < ''be-'' + ''leger'', a camp, encamping army, place to lie down, a bed (= E. ''lair'' and ''layer'' = G. ''lager'', a camp, = Sw. ''läger'', a bed, etc.): see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''leaguer'', ''ledger'', ''lair'', ''layer'', ''lager''.] To besiege; surround with an army so as to preclude escape; blockade.
{{smaller block|The Trojan camp, then ''beleaguered'' by Turnus and the Latins.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Dufresnoy.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' To invest, lay siege to, beset.}}

'''beleaguerer''' (bẹ̄-lē′gėr-ėr), ''n.'' One who beleaguers or besieges; a besieger.
{{smaller block|<poem>O’er the walls
The wild ''beleaguerers'' broke, and, one by one,
The strongholds of the plain were forced.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', The Prairies.}}}}

'''beleaguerment''' (bẹ̄-lē′gėr-ment), ''n.'' [< ''beleaguer'' + ''-ment''.] The act of beleaguering, or the state of being beleaguered.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fair, fickle, courtly France, . . .
Shattered by hard ''beleaguerment'', and wild ire,
That sacked and set her palaces on fire.</poem>
{{right|''R. H. Stoddard'', Guests of State.}}}}

'''beleave†''' (bē-lēv′), ''v.'' [< ME. ''beleven'', ''bileven'', etc., also by syncope ''bleven'', leave, intrans. remain, < AS. ''belǣfan'', leave, < ''be-'' + ''lǣfan'', leave; prop. the causal of ''belive''<sup>1</sup>, q. v. See ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''leave''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To leave behind; abandon; let go.
{{smaller block|There was nothynge ''belefte''. {{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., ii.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bekko-ware|511|beleave}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''bekko-ware''' (bek′ō-wãr), ''n.''   [< Jap. ''bekko'', tortoise-shell (< Chinese ''kwei'', tortoise, + ''kia'', armor), + ''ware''<sup>2</sup>.]   A kind of pottery anciently made in Japan, imitating tortoise-shell, or veined with green, yellow, and brown.

'''beknave''' (bē̤-nāv′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''beknaved'', ppr. ''beknaving''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''knave''.]   To call (one) a knave. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The lawyer ''beknaves'' the divine.{{right|''Gay'', Beggar’s Opera.}}}}

'''beknight''' (bē̤-nīt′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''knight''.]   '''1.''' To make a knight of. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The last ''beknighted'' booby.{{right|''T. Hook.''}}}}
'''2.''' To address as a knight, or by the title Sir.

'''beknit''' (bē̤-nit′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''knit''.]   To knit; girdle or encircle.
{{smaller block|Her filthy arms ''beknit'' with snakes about.{{right|''Golding'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph. (Ord MS.).}}}}

'''beknotted''' (bē̤-not′ed), ''a.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''knotted''.]   Knotted again and again; covered with knots.

'''beknottedness''' (bē̤-not′ed-nes), ''n.'' In ''math.'', the degree of complication of a knot; the number of times that it is necessary to pass one part of the curve of the knot projected upon a plane through another in order to untie the knot.

'''beknow†''' (bē̤-nō′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''beknowen'', ''biknowen'', < AS. ''becnāwan'', know, < ''be-'' + ''cnāwan'', know: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''know''.]   '''1.''' To know; recognize.—'''2.''' To acknowledge; own; confess. ''Ayenbyte of Inwyt'' (1340, ed. Morris).
{{smaller block|For I dare not ''beknowe'' min owen name.{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 698.}}}}

'''bel'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''a.''   [Early mod. E. also ''bell''; < ME. ''bele'', ''bel-'', < OF. (and mod. F.) ''bel'', ''beau'', fem. ''belle'', < L. ''bellus'', fair, fine, beautiful: see ''beau'', ''beauty'', ''bel''<sup>5</sup>, etc.]   '''1.''' Fair; fine; beautiful.—'''2.''' [Lit. fair, good, as in ''beausire'', fair sir, ''beaupere'', good father, used in F. and ME. to indicate indirect or adopted secondary relationship; so in mod. F. ''beau-'' as a formative in relation-names, ‘step-’, ‘-in-law’; ME. ''bel-'', ‘grand-’, as in ''beldame'', grandmother, ''belsire'', grandfather, also with purely E. names, ''belmoder'', ''belfader'', and later ''belchild''. Cf. Sc. and North. E. ''goodmother'', ''goodfather'', etc., mother-in-law, father-in-law, etc.] Grand-: a formative in relation-names, as ''belsire'', grandfather, ''beldam'', grandmother, etc. See etymology.

'''Bel'''<sup>2</sup> (bel), ''n.'' Same as ''Belus.''

'''bel'''<sup>3</sup> (bel), ''n.''   [Also written, less prop., ''bhel'', ''bael'', repr. Hind. ''bel.'']   The East Indian name of the Bengal quince-tree, ''Ægle Marmelos.'' See ''Ægle'', 1.

'''bela''' (bē′lä), ''n.''   [Hind.]   The Hindustani name of a species of jasmin, ''Jasminum Sambac'', which is often cultivated for its very fragrant flowers.

'''belabor, belabour''' (bē-lā′bo̤r), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''labor.'']   '''1†.''' To work hard upon; ply diligently.
{{smaller block|If the earth is ''belaboured'' with culture, it yieldeth corn.
{{right|''Barrow'', Works, III. xviii.}}}}
'''2.''' To beat soundly; thump.
{{smaller block|They so cudgelled and ''belabored'' him bodily that he might perhaps have lost his life in the encounter had he not been protected by the more respectable portion of the assembly.
{{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, I. 545.}}}}

'''bel-accoil†, bel-accoyle†''' (bel-a-koil′), ''n.''   [< OF. ''bel acoil'', fair welcome: see ''bel''<sup>1</sup> and ''accoil.'']   Kindly greeting or reception.   ''Spenser.''

'''belace<sup>1</sup>''' (bẹ̄-lās′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''lace.'']   '''1.''' To fasten as with a lace or cord.—'''2.''' To adorn with lace.
{{smaller block|<poem>When thou in thy bravest
And most ''belaced'' servitude dost strut,
Some newer fashion doth usurp.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, xvi. 10.}}}}
'''3†.''' To beat; whip.   ''Wright.''

'''belace<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' An error (by misprint or confusion with ''belace''<sup>1</sup>) in Bailey and subsequent dictionaries for ''belage'' or ''belay''. See ''belage''.

'''belacedness''' (bẹ̄-lā′sed-nes), ''n.'' In ''math.'', the number of times one branch of a lacing must be passed through another to undo it.

'''beladle''' (bẹ̄-lā′dl), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ladle.'']   To pour out with a ladle; ladle out.
{{smaller block|The honest masters of the roast ''beladling'' the dripping.
{{right|''Thackeray.''}}}}

'''belady''' (bẹ̄-lā′di), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''beladied'', ppr. ''beladying''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''lady''; cf. ''belord'', ''begrace'', ''beknight''.]   To address by the title Lady, or the phrase “my lady.”

'''belage†''', ''v.''   [Either a misprint for ''belaye'', ''belay'', or less prob. a phonetic variant of that word (ME. ''beleggen'', etc.): see ''belay''.]   ''Naut.'', to belay. ''Phillips'' (1678);   ''Kersey''.

'''belam''' (bẹ̄-lam′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''lam.'']   To beat; bang.   ''Sherwood.'' [North. Eng.]

'''belamour†''' (bel′a-mör), ''n.''   [Also ''bellamour'', < F. ''bel amour'', lit. fair love: see ''bel''<sup>1</sup> and ''amour''.]   '''1.''' A gallant; a consort.
{{smaller block|<poem>Loe, loe! how brave she decks her bounteous boure
With silkin curtens and gold coverletts,
Therein to shrowd her sumptuous ''Belamoure''.</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. vi. 16.}}}}
'''2.''' An old name for a flower which cannot now be identified.
{{smaller block|<poem>Her snowy browes, lyke budded ''Bellamoures''.</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, lxiv.}}}}

'''belamy†''' (bel′a-mi), ''n.''   [Early mod. E., also ''bellamy'', < ME. ''belamy'', ''belami'', < OF. ''bel ami'', fair friend: see ''bel''<sup>1</sup> and ''amy''.]   Good friend; fair friend: used principally in address.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou ''belamy'', thou pardoner, he seyde.</poem>{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Pardoner’s Tale, l. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nay, ''bellamy'', thou bus [must] be smytte.</poem>{{right|''York Plays'', p. 391.}}}}
{{smaller block|His dearest ''Belamy''. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. vii. 52.}}}}

'''belandre''' (bẹ̄-lan′dėr; F. pron. bā-loṅdr′), ''n.''   [F., < D. ''bijlander'', whence also E. ''bilander'', q. v.]   A small flat-bottomed craft, used principally on the rivers, canals, and roadsteads of France.

'''belate''' (bẹ̄-lāt′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''late''.]   To retard; make late; benight.
{{smaller block|<poem>The morn is young, quoth he,
A little time to old remembrance given
Will not ''belate'' us.</poem>{{right|''Southey'', Madoc, i. 10.}}}}

'''belated''' (bẹ̄-lā′ted), ''p. a.'' Coming or staying too late; overtaken by lateness, especially at night; benighted; delayed.
{{smaller block|<poem>Faery elves,
Whose midnight revels, by a forest side,</poem>}}
<poem>Or fountain, some ''belated'' peasant sees.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 783.}}}}

{{smaller block|Who were the parties? who inspected? who contested this ''belated'' account? {{right|''Burke'', Nabob of Arcot’s Debts.}}}}

'''belatedness''' (bē-lā′ted-nes), ''n.''   [< ''belated'', pp. of ''belate'', + ''-ness''.]   The state of being belated, or of being too late; slowness; backwardness.

{{smaller block|That you may see I am sometimes suspicious of myself, and do take notice of a certain ''belatedness'' in me, I am the bolder to send you some of my nightward thoughts.
{{right|''Milton'', Letter in Birch’s Life.}}}}

'''belaud''' (bē-lâd′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''laud''.]   To load with praise; laud highly.

{{smaller block|[Volumes] which were commended by divines from pulpits, and ''belauded'' all Europe over.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Virginians, xxvi.}}}}

'''belave''' (bē-lāv′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bilaven'', bathe, < ''bi-'', ''be-'' + ''laven'', lave: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''lave''<sup>1</sup>.]   To lave about; wash all over; wash.

'''belawgive†''' (bē-lâ′giv), ''v. t.''   [A forced word, used only in the passage from Milton, < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + *''lawgive'', assumed from ''lawgiver''.]   To give a law to.

{{smaller block|The Holy One of Israel hath ''belawgiven'' his own people with this very allowance. {{right|''Milton'', Divorce.}}}}

'''belay''' (bē-lā′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''beleggen'', ''bileggen'', < AS. ''belecgan'', lay upon, cover, charge (= D. ''beleggen'', cover, overlay; as a naut. term, belay; = OHG. ''bilegen'', MHG. G. ''belegen''), < ''be-'', about, around, by, + ''lecgan'', lay. The naut. use is perhaps due to the D. In the sense of ‘surround,’ cf. ''beleaguer''.]   '''1†.''' To surround; environ; inclose.—'''2†.''' To overlay; adorn.
<poem>All in a woodman’s jacket he was clad
Of Lincolne greene, ''belayd'' with silver lace.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. ii. 5.}}}}

'''3†.''' To besiege; invest; surround.

<poem>Gaynst such strong castles needeth greater might
Then those small forts which ye were wont ''belay''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, xiv.}}}}

<poem>So when Arabian thieves ''belayed'' us round.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Sandys'', Hymn to God.}}}}

'''4†.''' To lie in wait for in order to attack; hence, to block up or obstruct.

<poem>The speedy horse all passages ''belay''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, ix.}}}}

'''5.''' ''Naut.'', to fasten, or make fast, by winding {{img float|file=century v01 p0537 c2f1.png|width=195px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Belaying-pins in rail, with ropes belayed on them.}}}} round a belaying-pin, cleat, or cavel: applied chiefly to running rigging.

{{smaller block|When we ''belayed'' the halyards, there was nothing left but the bolt-rope.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before [the Mast, p. 256.}}}}

'''belaying-bitt''' (bẹ̄-lā′ing-bit), ''n.'' Any bitt to which a rope can be belayed.

'''belaying-pin''' (bẹ̄-lā′ing-pin), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', a wooden or iron pin to which running rigging may be belayed.

'''belch''' (belch), ''v.''   [Early mod. E., also ''belche'', ''bache'', < ME. ''belchen'', assibilated form of early mod. E. and E. dial. (north.) ''belk'', < ME. ''belken'', < AS. ''bælcian'', ''bealcian'', also with added formative, ''bealcettan'', belch, ejaculate; allied to ''balk''<sup>2</sup> and ''bolk'', all prob. ult. imitative: see ''belk'', ''balk''<sup>2</sup>, ''bolk''.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To eject wind noisily from the stomach through the mouth; eructate.
{{smaller block|All radishes breed wind, . . . and provoke a man that eateth them to ''belch''.{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xix. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' To issue out, as with eructation: as, “''belching'' flames,” ''Dryden''.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To throw or eject from the stomach with violence; eructate.
{{smaller block|''Belching'' raw gobbets from his maw.{{right|''Addison'', Æneid, iii.}}}}
'''2.''' To eject violently from within; cast forth.
{{smaller block|<poem>The gates, that now
Stood open wide, ''belching'' outrageous flame.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 232.}}}}
{{smaller block|Though heaven drop sulphur, and hell ''belch'' out fire.{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, ii. 2.}}}}
'''3.''' To ejaculate; vent with vehemence: often with ''out'': as, to ''belch out'' blasphemies; to ''belch out'' one’s fury.

'''belch''' (belch), ''n.''   [< ''belch'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act of throwing out from the stomach or from within; eructation.—'''2†.''' A cant name for malt liquor, from its causing belching.
{{smaller block|A sudden reformation would follow among all sorts of people; porters would no longer be drunk with ''belch''.{{right|''Dennis''.}}}}

'''belcher'''<sup>1</sup> (bel′chėr), ''n.'' One who belches.

'''belcher<sup>2</sup>''' (bel′chėr), ''n.''   [So called from an English pugilist named Jim ''Belcher''.]   A neckerchief with darkish-blue ground and large white spots with a dark-blue spot in the center of each. [Slang.]

'''belchild†''' (bel′child), ''n.''; pl. ''belchildren'' (-chil″-dre̤n).   [< ''bel-'', grand-, as in ''beldam'', ''belsire'', etc. (see ''bel''<sup>1</sup>), + ''child''.]   A grandchild.
{{smaller block|To Thomas Doubledaye and Katherine his wife, my daughter, a cowe. To their children, my ''belchildren'', etc.
{{right|''Will of'' 1564, quoted in N. and Q., 7th ser., III. 77.}}}}

'''beldam, beldame''' (bel′dam, -dām), ''n.''   [< ME. ''beldam'', ''beldame'', only in sense of grandmother (correlative to ''belsire'', grandfather), < ME. ''bel-'', grand-, as in ''belsire'', etc. (see ''bel''<sup>1</sup>), + ''dame'', mother. The word was thus in E. use lit. ‘good mother,’ used distinctively for grandmother, not as in F. ''belle dame'', lit. fair lady: see ''bel''<sup>1</sup>, ''belle'', and ''dame''.]   '''1†.''' Grandmother: corresponding to ''belsire'', grandfather: sometimes applied to a great-grandmother.
{{smaller block|To show the ''beldame'' daughters of her daughter.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 953.}}}}
'''2.''' An old woman in general, especially an ugly old woman; a hag.
{{smaller block|Around the ''beldam'' all erect they hang. {{right|''Akenside.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Our witches are no longer old
And wrinkled ''beldames'', Satan-sold.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', New-England Legend.}}}}
'''3†.''' [A forced use of the F. ''belle dame''.] Fair dame or lady. ''Spenser.''

'''belead†''', ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''beleden'', < AS. ''belǣdan'', < ''be-'' + ''lǣdan'', lead: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''lead''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' To lead away.—'''2.''' To lead; conduct.

'''beleaguer''' (bē-lē′gėr), ''v. t.''   [< D. ''belegeren'', besiege (= G. ''belagern'' = Sw. ''belägra'' = Dan. ''belægre'', also ''belejre'', perhaps < D. ''belegeren''), < ''be-'' + ''leger'', a camp, encamping army, place to lie down, a bed (= E. ''lair'' and ''layer'' = G. ''lager'', a camp, = Sw. ''läger'', a bed, etc.): see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''leaguer'', ''ledger'', ''lair'', ''layer'', ''lager''.]   To besiege; surround with an army so as to preclude escape; blockade.
{{smaller block|The Trojan camp, then ''beleaguered'' by Turnus and the Latins.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Dufresnoy.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' To invest, lay siege to, beset.}}

'''beleaguerer''' (bẹ̄-lē′gėr-ėr), ''n.'' One who beleaguers or besieges; a besieger.
{{smaller block|<poem>O’er the walls
The wild ''beleaguerers'' broke, and, one by one,
The strongholds of the plain were forced.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', The Prairies.}}}}

'''beleaguerment''' (bẹ̄-lē′gėr-ment), ''n.''   [< ''beleaguer'' + ''-ment''.]   The act of beleaguering, or the state of being beleaguered.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fair, fickle, courtly France, . . .
Shattered by hard ''beleaguerment'', and wild ire,
That sacked and set her palaces on fire.</poem>
{{right|''R. H. Stoddard'', Guests of State.}}}}

'''beleave†''' (bē-lēv′), ''v.''   [< ME. ''beleven'', ''bileven'', etc., also by syncope ''bleven'', leave, intrans. remain, < AS. ''belǣfan'', leave, < ''be-'' + ''lǣfan'', leave; prop. the causal of ''belive''<sup>1</sup>, q. v. See ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''leave''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To leave behind; abandon; let go.
{{smaller block|There was nothynge ''belefte''. {{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., ii.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
